messages.content: Predict the participant’s actual response in a laboratory study. Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 10 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 10 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 10 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 10 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 10 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 10 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 15 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 15 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 15 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 15 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 15 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 15 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 15 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 20 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 20 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 20 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 20 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 20 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 20 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 20 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 20 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 20 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 25 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 25 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 25 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 25 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 25 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 25 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 30 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 30 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 30 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 30 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 30 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. The divider to the paired person is removed: the observer can see the target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 30 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

The bicycle adds 10 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

You are the target. A divider blocks the observer’s view of the paired target, their screen and lights. The car would illuminate 4 lights, at about 3000 mg CO2/hour. The bicycle adds 25 seconds. Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
No individual background is supplied by these distribution constraints.

Participants receive a EUR 6 participation payment for a session of about 30 minutes and are randomly assigned as a target or observer. Adjacent target–observer pairs are assigned to an observable or non-observable arrangement of cubicle dividers. Targets complete a simulated transportation task with real waiting times and real unnecessary electricity consumption; observers evaluate music through headphones. Both roles are told what the two tasks involve and that the target’s car choice turns on energy-consuming lights. Observability means that behavior can be seen, without requiring constant attention to every choice. Each person can leave when their own tasks are finished. The target makes 40 car-or-bike choices in two blocks of 20. A car choice requires the displayed car waiting time and illuminates either 4 or 12 USB LED lights during that trip; a bicycle choice keeps the lights off but adds the displayed extra waiting time. The four-light rate is about 3000 mg CO2 per hour; the twelve-light rate is about 9000 mg per hour. These are emission rates, not emissions per trip. The bicycle option produces none of this additional light-related emission. Car waiting times are 5, 10, 15 or 20 seconds; the extra bicycle time is 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 seconds. Each combination occurs once per block in random order; block order is counterbalanced. Both absolute times and their difference are shown before an actual choice. There is no actual journey or per-choice monetary purchase. Return only car or bike.

Absolute car and bicycle times are unavailable at the retained aggregate resolution; the original participant did see them. Do not infer a particular absolute time or trial order. The retained record does not give this trial’s chronological position or preceding choice sequence. Their absence here does not mean the person did not know their own past choices.
